rationale: Aluminium in honey is low natural/environmental background. The pool requires reference-method restriction (logged as an outstanding item); the not-material determination rests on the ~5 mg/kg reference value, not the inflated 152.

rationale: No government sets a methylmercury ML for any grain, cereal, or rice product in any jurisdiction; methylmercury maximum levels exist only for fish and seafood. rationale: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in a non-root vegetable juice. At the pH of this product form (typically pH 3.9 to 4.6 for tomato-based juices and mildly acidic for other non-root vegetable juices, with organic acids and ascorbate present) Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by the organic acids, sugars, ascorbate and polyphenols present in the matrix, so a positive Cr(VI) result is an artifact of the total-chromium determination rather than a species present in the beverage as consumed. The reference-method basis for this determination is the in-house species arbitration at data/workbench/standards/2026-07-31-chromium-formula-adjudication.md, which found that the superseded ion-exchange plus electrothermal-AAS methods that generated the historical Cr(VI) values in liquid food matrices are not reproduced by the modern reference method: saraiva2021 (species-specific isotope dilution HPLC-ICP-MS, limit of quantification 0.049 ug/kg) quantified no Cr(VI) in any milk or formula sample while resolving Cr(III) and total chromium at single-digit ug/kg. That adjudication was drawn on a near-neutral aqueous food matrix; the acidic beverage matrices in this row are a more strongly reducing environment still, so the artifact conclusion carries a fortiori. The health-relevant species is controlled through the total-chromium cell and the reflex rule below, and this determination is a method finding, not an occurrence-derived value: no number is taken from it.

rationale: Mercury in sealed packaged drinking water is present essentially as inorganic Hg(II). Methylation is a microbial process requiring anaerobic sulfate- or iron-reducing activity in sediment or biota; it does not occur in a treated, filtered, disinfected and sealed packaged-water matrix, and there is no aquatic food chain in the product to bioaccumulate methylmercury. Methylmercury is in any event a component of total mercury, so it is bounded by identity at the published total-mercury ceiling of 1 µg/L. No separate methylmercury ceiling is published.
regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction in the register sets a methylmercury maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water: of the 27 methylmercury rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, every one is a fish or aquatic-animal tissue limit and none is water-scoped. Every drinking-water and packaged-water instrument in the pool regulates mercury as total mercury with no methyl line, and Hong Kong Cap 132V regulates the packaged-drinking-water mercury cell as INORGANIC mercury (0.006 mg/kg, hk_cap132v_ihg_bottled-or-packaged-drinking-waters-other-than-natural_6), which is direct sovereign confirmation that the regulated mercury species in packaged water is the inorganic one. The only methylmercury maxima anywhere in the register are fish and aquatic-animal limits (for example fda_cpg540600_mehg_fish_1000), which govern a bioaccumulating tissue matrix and have no application to water.

rationale: Methylmercury is a marine-bioaccumulation species. It has no formation route and no established industrial source in an infant or toddler bib: the mercury that can occur here comes from pigment, catalyst and preservative residues in coatings, polymers and dyestuffs, all of which are inorganic or aryl-mercury chemistries, and organomercury fungicides in these materials have been withdrawn across every jurisdiction checked. Every sovereign mercury instrument that reaches this article class is written on TOTAL mercury; not one sets a methylmercury value for an article, a coating or a textile. Methylmercury is a proper subset of total mercury by identity, so the mandatory total-mercury control on this row, together with the 10 mg/kg Canadian surface-coating-material companion ceiling that binds any print or applied film, bounds it absolutely and a separate methylmercury ceiling would add no protection.
regulatory_basis: No credible sovereign sets a methylmercury limit for an article, a surface coating or a textile. The mercury instruments that reach this category are Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5 (10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of surface coating material), Canada SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) (10 mg/kg total mercury in accessible toy coatings), the Australian Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2 toy-coating value (60 mg/kg, unspeciated) and Directive 2009/48/EC Annex II Part III (total-mercury migration) — all total-element.

rationale: No credible sovereign sets an inorganic-arsenic limit for a textile. REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12, the instrument that governs this row, limits arsenic compounds expressed as As metal — a total-element value, as the register records — and every other arsenic instrument that reaches a children's article is likewise unspeciated. Inorganic arsenic is a proper subset of total arsenic by identity, so the published 1 mg/kg extractable total-arsenic ceiling on this same row bounds it absolutely and a separate inorganic ceiling would add no protection. Arsenic-based dyestuffs are obsolete in every jurisdiction checked and no residual arsenical finishing chemistry is in commercial use for infant textiles.

rationale: No credible sovereign sets an inorganic-arsenic limit for a textile. Arsenic-based dyestuffs are obsolete in every jurisdiction checked and no residual arsenical finishing chemistry is in commercial use for infant apparel.

rationale: Hexavalent chromium is not stable in this matrix. Raw and cooked red-meat muscle tissue is a wet, reducing, protein- and thiol-rich medium; Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) by tissue reductants (cysteine, glutathione, ascorbate) and by the acid and heat of digestion and cooking, so a Cr(VI) figure reported on such a matrix is an artifact of the extraction chemistry of the total-chromium screen rather than a measurement of a species that persists in the food. The determination follows the same reference-method adjudication recorded for the hexavalent-chromium cell in the infant-formula category (data/workbench standards Cr-VI adjudication), applied here to an animal-tissue matrix. Hexavalent chromium is in any event a species of, and bounded by, the published total-chromium screen (Cr-VI <= total Cr).
regulatory_basis: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium content limit for any food. Every credible Cr(VI) instrument on the register is an article, textile, leather, toy-migration, tattoo-ink, fertiliser or electrical-equipment limit in a non-food basis, and applying one to a food matrix would be a basis conflation the compiler's basis guard rejects. Total chromium is regulated for meat and poultry by Hong Kong Cap. 132V and is published here as a screen.

rationale: Aluminium is the PERMITTED ACTIVE INGREDIENT of an antiperspirant, not a contaminant of it. Aluminium chlorohydrate, aluminium chloride, aluminium sesquichlorohydrate and aluminium zirconium tetrachlorohydrex glycine are the astringent actives that make the product work; the US over-the-counter antiperspirant monograph at 21 CFR 350 lists them as permitted actives and regulates their concentration as an active-ingredient specification expressed in percent of the anhydrous salt, and the EU restricts the aluminium zirconium complexes as ingredients under Regulation 1223/2009 Annex III. Neither is an impurity ceiling. Publishing a total-aluminium contaminant maximum for this form would be a category error: every compliant product would exceed any contaminant-scale value by three to four orders of magnitude, so the number would police the label claim rather than any contamination, and a brand could satisfy it only by removing the active. No credible sovereign publishes an aluminium contaminant maximum for an antiperspirant or for any other cosmetic form.

rationale: Methylmercury is a component of total mercury and cannot exceed it by identity, and a leave-on cosmetic matrix supplies no methylation pathway: biotic mercury methylation requires the sulfate- and iron-reducing microbial activity of anoxic aquatic sediment, which has no analogue in an anhydrous, emulsified or preserved cosmetic formulation. The published total-mercury ceiling on this row therefore bounds methylmercury completely, so no separate methylmercury ceiling is published.

rationale: Methylmercury is formed by microbial methylation in aquatic sediments and food webs and reaches humans by bioaccumulation in fish and shellfish muscle. A surfactant-based rinse-off cosmetic has no methylation pathway, no aquatic food-web input and no dietary mercury route; mercury that reaches such a product arrives as inorganic mercury from pigments and raw-material impurities, or illegally as an inorganic skin-lightening active. Cosmetic mercury surveys accordingly measure and report total mercury, not methylmercury. Any mercury present is governed by, and bounded by identity below, the published total-mercury ceiling of 100 µg/kg, so a separate methylmercury ceiling would add nothing. This determination is rebuttable: a routed occurrence source reporting methylmercury in a rinse-off cosmetic at material levels retires it and the cell reverts to a control.

rationale: Inorganic arsenic is the toxic fraction of total arsenic and a species of it (iAs <= tAs). The inorganic fraction is therefore governed by, and bounded by, the total-arsenic ceiling published on the tAs cell of this row. The determination is a governance statement about which cell carries the ceiling, not an assertion that inorganic arsenic is absent, and it is rebuttable: the only routed inorganic-arsenic measurement anywhere in this category's evidence base is zhang2026-cotton-arsenic-amf-calcium, which speciates inorganic arsenic in COTTON FIBRE as a soil-uptake pathway in the textile substrate, not as a contaminant of a product applied to the textile, so it does not rebut this determination for the product itself. rationale: Methylmercury is formed by microbial methylation in aquatic food chains, where an anaerobic sulfate- or iron-reducing microbial community acts on a bioavailable inorganic-mercury pool over long residence times. This row's THREE named material configurations are each addressed rather than covered by a single clause. An aluminised, tinned, aluminium or carbon-steel pan is a metal surface with no organic matrix and no methylation pathway. A moulded SILICONE bakeware article and a non-stick or silicone-release COATING are cured synthetic polymers: they are organic, but they are crosslinked solids with no bioavailable carbon substrate for a methylating community, they are used in dry, aerobic, high-temperature baking contact rather than in a submerged anoxic environment, and they carry no inorganic-mercury pool to methylate. A GLASS or CERAMIC baking dish is a fired inorganic matrix with no organic carbon at all. None of the three supplies a methyl donor to mercury, and the baking contact conditions this row certifies — high temperature, short duration, washed and dried between uses — are the opposite of the conditions methylation requires. No credible sovereign sets a methylmercury requirement for any food-contact material in any basis. Total mercury is the governing determination for this row and remains a mandatory control on every configuration; methylmercury is not material and never substitutes for it.

bounded_by: tHg (read-across of eu_10_2011_thg_sml_nd, total mercury not detectable at 0.01 mg/kg food)
rationale: Methylmercury is formed by microbial methylation in aquatic food chains, where an anaerobic sulfate- or iron-reducing microbial community acts on a bioavailable inorganic-mercury pool over residence times measured in weeks to years. The determination on this row is argued from THIS ROW'S OWN MATERIALS rather than from a generic cured-polymer clause. A moulded HDPE or polypropylene board is a cured synthetic polymer with no organic carbon available to a methylating community. The row's other named configurations are not polymers and are addressed directly: end-grain and edge-grain hardwood boards, bamboo boards bonded with urea- or phenol-formaldehyde adhesive, resin-and-paper composite boards and rubber-wood or epoxy-embedded decorative boards are organic, wettable matrices that absorb food once knife-scored, so the absence of a methylation pathway has to be established for them rather than assumed. It rests on the contact conditions actually certified: domestic board use is a short, aerobic, repeatedly washed and dried contact, with no persistent anaerobic niche and no sulfate-reducing or iron-reducing community established in the matrix, and contact duration is orders of magnitude shorter than methylation kinetics in a sediment or water column. There is in addition no substrate to methylate: neither the lignocellulosic matrix nor the formaldehyde-resin adhesive line carries a bioavailable inorganic-mercury pool, and neither supplies a methyl donor to mercury. No credible sovereign sets a methylmercury requirement for a food-contact material of any family in any basis. The total-mercury requirement on this row is a published non-detect value rather than a control, so any organomercury fraction is bounded by a real number, and boards are tested for total mercury AFTER the declared scoring conditioning, so the bound is measured on the scored, food-absorbing surface rather than on an as-supplied one. Methylmercury is not material and never substitutes for the total-mercury cell.
regulatory_basis: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2 sets the element requirement as a specific migration requirement on the food or food simulant, not as a limit on the material's element content. No credible sovereign sets a species-specific migration limit for this cell. Wood and bamboo are Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material families for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, and no credible-set jurisdiction sets a methylmercury requirement for them or for any other food-contact material family.

rationale: Methylmercury is formed by microbial methylation in aquatic sediment and biomagnifies through aquatic food webs. This row's emitting material is a manufactured non-marine formulation (the additive as supplied, homogenised across the retail unit, with the friable fines fraction analysed separately) with no methylation pathway, no aquatic trophic transfer and no marine-derived or wild-harvested animal input, and methylmercury is in any event a component of total mercury, so MeHg is less than or equal to tHg by identity and is bounded by and controlled through the published total-mercury ceiling of 100 ug/kg. Methylmercury is additionally thermally labile and decomposes well below the temperatures reached in any heated or combustion form in this category, so no thermal pathway creates it either. No credible sovereign government sets a methylmercury limit for any air-care product, and no routed occurrence source reports methylmercury in one, which is the speciation-aware condition the not-material integrity gate applies. No separate methylmercury ceiling is published because none would bind below the total-mercury ceiling.
